passage: Jahnavi knew every answer in Class 5, but she dreaded roll call. Her name began with a sound that got stuck. So each morning, when Vandana Ma'am called "Jahnavi?", she said "Present" through a cough, or just raised her hand. In reading hour she swapped words to dodge the hard ones: "big" instead of "huge", "later" instead of "tomorrow". Sometimes the sentence came out strange. A boy at the back started copying her, "J-j-j-jahnavi," and she stared at her desk until her eyes burned. That night her mother held her and listened to all of it. On Saturday they went to a qualified speech therapist near the station, who showed Jahnavi how to ease into a word gently. On Monday, her mother spoke to Vandana Ma'am about the boy.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say instead of 'huge' in reading hour?
qa.a: Big.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi dread roll call?
qa.a: She feared getting stuck on her own name in front of the class and being laughed at.

qa.q: Which choices by her mother helped?
qa.a: She listened to all of it, took Jahnavi to a qualified speech therapist, and told the teacher about the teasing.

qa.q: How might Vandana Ma'am's classroom change once she knows about the teasing?
qa.a: She can stop the copying and give Jahnavi time, so roll call feels less frightening.

grounding: It shows a child who avoids reading aloud, swaps words to dodge hard sounds and dreads being called on, worsened by teasing and helped by speech therapy.

passage: "Omkar, stay a minute?" Gurleen Ma'am said as the others filed out. "D-d-did I do something?" "No. I noticed you didn't volunteer for the play reading. Would you like to tell me why?" He twisted his tie. "I g-get stuck. And then R-Rohit's gang does the noise." "Thank you for telling me. That noise stops today; I'll speak to them. Now, what would make reading easier for you?" "If I kn-know which part the day before. And if nobody hurries me." "Done. I'll give you your part tomorrow, and I'll wait as long as it takes. Your speech therapist on Wednesdays, would it help if I knew what she's practising with you?" Omkar looked up for the first time. "Yeah. That would help." "Good. I'd like to hear your part in the play."

qa.q: On which day does Omkar see his speech therapist?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: Why did Omkar avoid volunteering for the play reading?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting stuck and of Rohit's gang making the noise to mock him.

qa.q: What steps did Gurleen Ma'am agree to take?
qa.a: Stop the teasing, give him his part the day before, wait as long as it takes, and learn what the therapist is practising.

qa.q: How does Omkar's attitude change during the talk?
qa.a: At first he twists his tie and avoids her eyes, but by the end he looks up and agrees it would help.

grounding: It shows a child who dreads reading aloud because of stuttering and teasing, and a teacher who allows time and works alongside his speech therapist.

passage: In the government school near Hassan, Madhuri, ten, counted the rows ahead of her during reading time, working out which paragraph would be hers. It started with "Monday." She practised under her breath: "The first day of the week." Her stomach twisted. When Kashish, at the next desk, copied her stutter at lunch, Madhuri stopped talking altogether for a week. Her teacher, Shobha Ma'am, noticed. She told Kashish firmly that mocking was not allowed, and told Madhuri, "You can take as long as you need. We will wait." Twice a month, a speech therapist visited the primary health centre, and Madhuri's mother began taking her there. Slowly, reading time became something she could face.

qa.q: How did Madhuri plan to avoid saying "Monday"?
qa.a: She planned to say "The first day of the week" instead.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel during reading time?
qa.a: She felt afraid and dreaded it, counting rows ahead and feeling her stomach twist.

qa.q: What steps helped Madhuri?
qa.a: Her teacher stopped the mocking and gave her time, and she began seeing a speech therapist at the primary health centre.

qa.q: How might Kashish's copying have affected Madhuri?
qa.a: It made things worse, hurting and shaming her so much that she stopped talking for a week.

grounding: Shows a child who dreads reading aloud and swaps words to avoid sounds, made worse by teasing, and helped by a patient teacher and a speech therapist.

passage: In Durban, Zanele, eleven, woke with a stomach ache every Thursday: oral report day. She wrote her talks full of easy words, "talk" instead of "presentation," "big" instead of "enormous," because P and E sounds got stuck. When a boy laughed at her last time, she wanted to disappear. On Tuesday afternoons she saw Siddiq, a speech therapist at the community clinic, who helped her practise gently and never mocked. This week her teacher, Mrs Dube, said, "Zanele, you can go last, and take all the time you need." Zanele spoke for three minutes about her grandmother's garden. She stuck on "tomatoes" twice. Nobody laughed. She sat down with her hands still shaking, but smiling.

qa.q: On which afternoons did Zanele see Siddiq?
qa.a: She saw Siddiq on Tuesday afternoons.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel about oral report day?
qa.a: She dreaded it and felt afraid, waking with a stomach ache every Thursday.

qa.q: What helped Zanele give her report?
qa.a: Practice with a qualified speech therapist, and a teacher who let her go last and take all the time she needed.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dube feel watching Zanele sit down smiling?
qa.a: Mrs Dube may feel glad and proud that giving Zanele time helped her get through the report.

grounding: Shows a child who dreads speaking, swaps words to dodge sounds and is hurt by teasing, and is helped by a teacher allowing time and speech therapy.

passage: At roll call in Class 4, Pallavi, nine, never said "Present." She said "Yes, Ma'am," because the P got stuck. On reading days she had tummy aches and asked to go to the sick room. Reena Ma'am noticed the pattern. One morning she kept Pallavi back after assembly. "Would you like to read your part to me alone first, before class?" Pallavi nodded, eyes on her shoes. When she read in class later and a boy sniggered, Reena Ma'am said, "We wait for everyone here," and waited with the class. Pallavi also started Saturday sessions with a speech therapist her parents found through the school. By the end of term, she said "Present" once. Quietly, but she said it.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say instead of "Present" at roll call?
qa.a: She said "Yes, Ma'am."

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel on reading days?
qa.a: She felt fearful and anxious, getting tummy aches and asking to go to the sick room.

qa.q: What did Reena Ma'am do to make speaking less frightening?
qa.a: She let Pallavi read to her alone first, stopped the sniggering and made the whole class wait patiently.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's parents feel when she says "Present" at last?
qa.a: They may feel proud and hopeful, seeing the speech therapy and teacher support begin to help.

grounding: Shows a child who swaps words, avoids reading aloud and dreads being called on, helped by a patient teacher who stops teasing and by a speech therapist.

passage:
Tuesday. Jaya's stomach knotted as the reading round moved down the row. She said "I feel sick" and went to the washroom before her turn. When she had to answer the attendance, she said "present" instead of "yes, Ma'am" because "y" often got stuck.
Friday. Saurabh copied her in the corridor: "P-p-present!" Jaya didn't speak in class at all that day.
The next Wednesday. Mrs Dutta, the class teacher, had spoken to Saurabh, and he said sorry. She told Jaya she could read in her own time, with no rushing and no one finishing words. Jaya also had her first session with a speech therapist at the city hospital. That afternoon she read two lines aloud. It was slow. Nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did Jaya say instead of "yes, Ma'am" at attendance?
qa.a: She said "present".

qa.q: How did Jaya feel as the reading round moved down the row?
qa.a: She felt afraid and dreaded her turn, with her stomach knotting so she made an excuse to leave.

qa.q: What helped Jaya read aloud again?
qa.a: The teacher stopped the teasing, gave her time without rushing, and she began sessions with a speech therapist.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see things differently after Mrs Dutta spoke to him?
qa.a: He may realise his copying hurt Jaya and made speaking even harder for her.

grounding: Jaya avoids reading aloud, swaps words and dreads being called on; teasing makes it worse, and teacher patience plus a speech therapist help.
